overview.title: 📖 Overview: Opening Masechet Temurah
overview.subtitle: Temurah 2a–2b
overview.hebrewSource: הַכֹּל מְמִירִין, אֶחָד אֲנָשִׁים וְאֶחָד נָשִׁים
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Masechet Temurah opens with the mishna's declaration that 'everyone' substitutes a non-sacred animal for a consecrated one — the substitution takes effect even though it is forbidden, and the substituter is flogged. The Gemara first resolves the mishna's apparent self-contradiction (does 'everyone substitutes' mean it is permitted?) using Rav Yehuda's reading and the verse in Leviticus 27:10. It then works through who exactly is included in 'everyone': an inheritor (disputed by Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda, each deriving the end of consecration from its beginning or vice versa), a woman (included via a doubled verb or an added conjunction), and finally raises open dilemmas about minors and gentiles that carry into the next daf.

slides.title: ⚖️ Resolving the Mishna's Contradiction
slides.subtitle: 'Everyone substitutes' sounds permitted; 'if he substituted' sounds forbidden

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: This mishna is self-contradictory: 'הַכֹּל מְמִירִין' implies substitution may be done ab initio, but then it says 'if one substituted' — only after the fact!

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: And how could you even think 'everyone substitutes' means ab initio? The verse itself says: לֹא יַחֲלִיפֶנּוּ וְלֹא יָמִיר אֹתוֹ, 'he shall not alter it, nor substitute it' (Leviticus 27:10)!

lines.speaker: Rav Yehuda
lines.text: Read the mishna this way: 'Everyone can apply consecrated status to a non-sacred animal' by substitution — not that it is permitted, but that if one did it, the substitution takes effect and he is flogged.

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: Temurah is a case where a forbidden act nonetheless achieves its result — the animal becomes consecrated even as the act is punished.

slides.title: 👨‍👩‍👧 Does an Inheritor Substitute?
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda argue by comparing the start and end of consecration

boxes.title: Rabbi Meir
items: An inheritor places hands (semikha) on an inherited offering
Derives end-of-consecration (semikha) from the beginning (temurah): since an heir substitutes, he also places hands

boxes.title: Rabbi Yehuda
items: An inheritor does not place hands
Derives beginning (temurah) from the end (semikha): since an heir does not place hands, he also cannot substitute

callout.label: Mishna's ruling:
callout.text: Since our mishna's 'everyone' includes the inheritor, it follows Rabbi Meir, not Rabbi Yehuda.

slides.title: 📜 Deriving Semikha From 'His Offering'
slides.subtitle: The word קׇרְבָּנוֹ appears three times regarding placing hands on a peace offering

nodes.content: ❓ From where do we derive that only the owner places hands (semikha)?

columns.label: Instance 1
columns.content: His offering — not a gentile's offering

columns.label: Instance 2
columns.content: His offering — not another's offering (only the owner)

columns.label: Instance 3
columns.content: His offering — not his father's offering (an heir cannot place hands)

nodes.content: 🔀 Rabbi Meir needs the third instance for joint owners (בַּעֲלֵי חוֹבְרִין) instead, so for him an heir can place hands

callout.label: Note:
callout.text: Rabbi Yehuda holds joint owners are not included at all, since their offering is not 'his own' individually.

slides.title: 🙋 Including a Woman in the Prohibition
slides.subtitle: Two tannaim, two different textual hooks for the same conclusion
rows: The doubled verb אִם הָמֵר יָמִיר
Includes a woman, since the passage otherwise speaks only in the masculine
Includes a woman; he does not need the doubled verb for this, using it instead for an inheritor
Numbers 5:6, 'a man or woman' — general equation of punishments
Not sufficient here, since temurah is a punishment that does not apply equally to everyone (the public and partners are excluded, 13a)

callout.label: Why a special verse was needed:
callout.text: Since the general rule equating men and women applies only to punishments that apply equally to all, and temurah's flogging does not apply to the community or to partners, a woman's liability needed its own textual source.

slides.title: 👶🌍 Open Dilemmas: Minor and Gentile
slides.subtitle: Rami bar Ḥama's questions, framed by the halakhot of consecration

steps.content: 1️⃣ A minor who reached 'the age of vows' (עוֹנַת נְדָרִים) can consecrate an animal as a mufla — 'shall clearly utter' (Leviticus 27:2) includes him
2️⃣ Question: since he can consecrate, can he also effect substitution — even though minors are not subject to punishments?
3️⃣ Similarly: 'ish ish' — 'any man' — includes gentiles, who can bring vow and gift offerings like a Jew
4️⃣ Question: since a gentile's consecration takes effect, can he also effect substitution, though he too is never subject to Torah punishments?

callout.label: Rava's answer for the gentile (from a baraita):
callout.text: A baraita on animals consecrated by gentiles states plainly: אֵין עוֹשִׂין תְּמוּרָה — they do not effect substitution — though Rabbi Yosei limits Rabbi Shimon's leniency about misuse to altar-consecrations.

summary.principle: Temurah is forbidden yet effective: 'everyone' who substitutes — man, woman, or (disputed) an inheritor — is flogged, but the non-sacred animal still becomes consecrated.

flowSteps.content: 🐑 Mishna: everyone substitutes; not permitted, but if done it takes effect and incurs 40 lashes
⚖️ Rav Yehuda resolves the contradiction: 'everyone can apply consecrated status' — descriptive, not permissive

columns.content: 👨‍👩‍👧 R' Meir: heir substitutes and places hands; R' Yehuda: neither
🙋 Woman included via doubled verb or extra conjunction

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: 'Everyone' in the mishna is scrutinized word by word — each included or excluded party has its own verse

quiz.q: According to Rav Yehuda's resolution of the mishna's apparent contradiction, what does 'everyone substitutes' mean?
o: It is fully permitted to substitute
Everyone can apply consecrated status to a non-sacred animal via substitution, though it is forbidden and punished
Only priests may substitute
Substitution never actually takes effect
quiz.e: Rav Yehuda reads the mishna as describing the outcome (the status takes effect) while the act itself remains forbidden and flogged, resolving the apparent contradiction with the following clause.

quiz.q: What verse does the Gemara cite to show that substitution is forbidden?
o: "You shall not muzzle an ox"
"He shall not alter it, nor substitute it" (Leviticus 27:10)
"An eye for an eye"
"You shall not boil a kid in its mother's milk"
quiz.e: Leviticus 27:10, 'לֹא יַחֲלִיפֶנּוּ וְלֹא יָמִיר אֹתוֹ', explicitly prohibits substitution, which is why 'everyone substitutes' cannot mean it is permitted ab initio.

quiz.q: What is Rabbi Yehuda's reasoning for ruling that an inheritor cannot effect substitution?
o: He derives the beginning of consecration (temurah) from its end (semikha): just as an heir does not place hands, he cannot substitute
He says women cannot inherit sacrifices
He holds inheritors are exempt from all mitzvot
He derives it from the word 'ish ish'
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda reasons from the end of consecration (placing hands before slaughter, which an heir cannot do) to its beginning (substitution), concluding an heir cannot do either.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Meir derive that a woman is included in the prohibition against substitution?
o: From the doubled verb 'אִם הָמֵר יָמִיר'
From the extra conjunction 'וְאִם' ("and if")
From Numbers 5:6 alone
He does not include women at all
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir derives a woman's inclusion from the added 'and' (וְאִם), since he uses the doubled verb 'hamer yamir' instead to include the inheritor.

quiz.q: What does the baraita that Rava cites conclude about a gentile who consecrates an animal?
o: A gentile's consecration is entirely void
A gentile effects substitution just like a Jew
Gentiles do not effect substitution (אֵין עוֹשִׂין תְּמוּרָה) for what they consecrate
Only Rabbi Yosei says gentiles cannot substitute
quiz.e: The baraita states plainly that consecrated animals of gentiles do not undergo temurah, which Rava brings as evidence resolving Rami bar Ḥama's dilemma in the case where the gentile both consecrates and seeks atonement himself.
